summary:
Somalia criminalises same-sex sexual activity, and the sources give irreconcilable penalties. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records a maximum of life imprisonment under a penal code it dates to 1964, together with the death penalty under sharia in some regions. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report gives up to three years, while its 2022 report gives three months to three years for "carnal intercourse with a person of the same sex", with no official reports of enforcement available for that year.

Article 409 of the penal code, dated to 1973, sets three months to three years for sexual intercourse with a person of the same sex and two months to two years for an "act of lust" other than intercourse. Article 410 permits an additional security measure, usually police surveillance, intended to prevent re-offending.

Under local interpretations of sharia, homosexuality is punishable by death. The 2022 State Department report states that no known state-conducted executions of that kind were reported and that impunity generally remained the norm, while the same report and an encyclopaedia entry record capital punishment being imposed for consensual same-sex sexual activity in areas under insurgent control and in Jubaland, at a judge's discretion. The 2021 report separately records that the insurgent group al-Shabaab enforces strict sharia in which death is a possible punishment.

An international LGBT rights organisation reports killings by al-Shabaab or other non-state armed groups of people alleged to have engaged in homosexual activity: two male teenagers aged 15 and 18 together with a man aged 20 in 2017, a young man in 2018, and two men executed by al-Shabaab in 2024. The 2024 case is the most recent documented instance in this record; no later instance is documented. The sources give no denominator and no per-capita comparison, so these raw counts cannot be ranked against other jurisdictions or read against the country's general conflict death rate.

In government-controlled areas, civil law specifies prison sentences of up to three years and LGBTQ people are regularly prosecuted. The law does not prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, as the US Department of State reported in 2022.

The Marriage Law of 1974 defines marriage as "a contract between a man and a woman having equal rights and duties with the object of creating a family", which excludes same-sex unions from legal recognition.

Sexual orientation is a taboo subject with no public discussion in any region of the country, per US Department of State reports from 2010 and 2022, and severe societal stigma prevented LGBTQI+ individuals from making their sexual orientation or gender identity known publicly as of 2022. Stigmatisation and criminalisation operate in a country where 99% of the population follows Islam amid decades of civil war and unstable government.

Family planning services and factual information on human sexuality are hard to access, and Islamic social mores often make it difficult to discuss HIV transmission publicly. Since 1999, much AIDS/HIV education and care has come from international organisations such as the United Nations; Somalia has one of the lowest HIV infection rates on the continent, with adult prevalence estimated at 0.5% in 2007.
tangentialFactors:
The operating environment recorded in the 2021 State Department report is one of pervasive violence and statelessness, and the archived 2010 report documents the conflict and al-Shabaab abuses alongside its LGBT section. Which penalty applies, and whether the penalty is prison or death, depends on whether the territory involved is under government control or under insurgent control; the sources describe two parallel legal regimes rather than one.

The 2016 report by Benjamin Christman on the treatment of gay persons in Somalia, covered by Erasing 76 Crimes on 16 February 2016, sets out evidence that gay persons should not be returned to Somalia because of persecution risk, supporting refugee-status claims and forming a non-refoulement basis for LGBT asylum seekers. An Al Jazeera feature of July 2013 records Somali refugees in Kenya facing death threats and racist discrimination, al-Shabaab publicising an intent to enforce harsh punishments against homosexuality, and senior figures claiming a "death chamber" for gay and lesbian people if they were returned, while UN officials nevertheless pushed return.

Human rights and LGBTQ activists, and those accused of homosexuality, have been forced to flee the country for fear of execution or assassination. Any single penalty figure quoted for Somalia should be attributed to its source, because the 1964 penal code, the 1973 penal code and the State Department reports give different ranges for the same conduct.
localsOnly:
Prosecutions of LGBTQ people are described as regular in government-controlled areas, where civil law specifies prison terms of up to three years, and Article 410 allows an additional security measure, usually police surveillance, after sentence. Reporting on one's sexual orientation or gender identity publicly was not something LGBTQI+ individuals could do as of 2022 because of the severity of societal stigma, and sexual orientation remains without public discussion in any region of the country.

Organised community infrastructure is thin: as of 2004 one group reportedly existed for LGBTQ people in Somalia, and by 2022 there were few, very discreet, mostly online-based LGBTQI+ organisations holding events. Since 1999, much of the country's AIDS/HIV education and care has been delivered by international organisations such as the United Nations, against a setting where family planning services and factual information on human sexuality are hard to access and where Islamic social mores make public discussion of HIV transmission difficult.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no trans-specific legal provision, incident or survey. Every documented offence, killing and prosecution concerns sexual orientation or same-sex conduct; gender identity appears only in the 2022 finding that the law does not prohibit discrimination on that ground. Trans-specific exposure in Somalia is therefore not separately sourced here and remains unresolved.

No source in this inventory addresses entry or visa rules, passport or gender-marker handling, airport or checkpoint screening, detention facilities, bathroom access, or restrictions on gender-affirming care. Those questions are not sourced rather than answered.

The penalty range is unresolved: the Human Dignity Trust profile gives life imprisonment under a 1964 penal code, the 2021 State Department report gives up to three years, the 2022 report and Article 409 give three months to three years, and the death penalty is reported under sharia in some regions. The sources do not reconcile which instrument governs. Enforcement data is also absent for 2022, where the State Department reports no official reports of enforcement, and no source states how often the Article 410 surveillance measure is applied.

The documented killings are reported as raw counts with no population denominator, and no trans-specific or per-capita rate appears in any source, so their magnitude relative to other jurisdictions or to the country's general homicide rate cannot be established.
